paras: The shooting of Richard Williams took place in Kansas City on May 1, 1882, when Warren Landers, a clerk in a shoe house, shot Williams, a Black porter. The quarrel was said to have begun when Landers walked through a pile of dirt the porter had swept up, and Landers fled to Kentucky afterward. The shooting reached readers outside Missouri only as a brief wire item that did not report Williams's condition.

According to a National Associated Press dispatch datelined Kansas City, May 1, Landers, described as a clerk in "a prominent shoe house of this city," shot "the colored porter, Richard Williams" that day. The dispatch traced "the trouble" to Landers "walking through a pile of dirt that had been swept up by the porter," without saying what words or blows passed between the two men before the shot. It did not say where Williams was hit, how badly he was hurt, or whether he survived.

Landers fled to Pembroke, Kentucky, where he had formerly lived, and the dispatch added that his parents were "reported as being wealthy." No report of an arrest, extradition, inquest or trial was found in the coverage.

The Omaha Daily Bee printed the dispatch on its front page on May 2 under the headline "He Popped and Fled," among a column of short wire items on a smallpox outbreak, a duel, a boxing match and a burglar's escape. The item named the victim's race and the shooter's family wealth but gave no detail on the victim himself beyond his job. No other paper's account, and no Kansas City report, was found.
